strengths: Resolves, for the broad class of M-convex action sets (including all matroid bases), a genuinely open question in online inverse linear optimization: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in d is achievable. The O(d log d) bound is a substantial improvement over the prior finite bound exp(O(d log d)) of Gollapudi et al. (2021), and the paper is honest that this is only a partial resolution of the general question.

The technical development is clean and self-contained: the warm-up O(d^2) algorithm via pairwise-order learning (Theorem 3.1) makes the core M-convexity insight (Proposition 2.4) transparent, and the refinement to O(d log d) via a Grünbaum-theorem volume argument on the order-constrained polytope P_t (Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2) is elegant and correct. The lower bound on Vol(P_T) via the Freudenthal order-simplex triangulation is a nice touch.

The corruption-robust extension is a genuinely novel use of the structure: monitoring acyclicity of the directed graph ([d], A_t) both detects corruptions (Lemma 5.1) and certifies no-regret rounds (Lemma 5.2), yielding O((C+1)d log d) without prior knowledge of C via restarts. The proof carefully verifies that Lemma 4.1 does not rely on feedback optimality, and the accounting that each restart consumes a distinct corrupted round is correct.

The Ω(d) lower bound for the M-convex case (via embedding the M♮-convex segment instances of Sakaue et al. 2025b into Z^{d+1}) shows the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor, giving a nearly complete picture for this setting.

Well written and well organized; computational issues are addressed honestly (exact center of gravity is #P-hard, approximate computation via known randomized algorithms; complexity of graph updates and cycle detection is analyzed). Assumptions (per-round O(1) regret, distinct components of w*) are standard and their justification is given.
weaknesses: The contribution is restricted to M-convex action sets; the general open question (finite polynomial regret for arbitrary feasible sets) remains open, and the techniques appear to depend heavily on the M-convex exchange structure, so the scope of the resolution is partial.

The main ingredients are combinations of known techniques: pairwise-order learning with a volume argument borrows from contextual search/pricing (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Paes Leme & Schneider 2022), and the lower bound is an adaptation of Sakaue et al. (2025b). The novelty lies mainly in the synthesis with M-convexity and the cycle-based corruption detection, which is real but somewhat incremental.

No empirical evaluation or case study is provided; the practical relevance of the M-convex setting (matroids, resource allocation) is argued but not demonstrated. Also, practical usability is limited by the need for approximate center-of-gravity computation and membership-oracle access to M-convex sets, which may be nontrivial for large instances.

The corruption model counts rounds with non-optimal actions (a relatively restrictive notion); the more flexible cumulative-suboptimality corruption framework of Sakaue et al. (2025b) is not handled, which the authors acknowledge as future work.

Some details are deferred or lightly argued, e.g., the tie-breaking perturbation's effect on the volume argument is handled by citing the approximate Grünbaum theorem without full quantification of constants, and the lower-bound proof is brief, relying on verifying an adaptation of a prior argument.

strengths: Resolves, for an important and broad class of action sets (M-convex sets, which subsume matroid bases such as m-sets and spanning trees), an explicitly posed open question from Gollapudi et al. (2021) and Sakaue et al. (2025b): whether a finite regret bound polynomial in d is achievable. The O(d log d) bound is tight up to a log d factor given the adapted Ω(d) lower bound (Theorem 6.1).

The technical development is clean and correct as far as I can verify: the warm-up O(d²) argument via the exchange characterization (Proposition 2.4) is sound, and the refinement in Section 4 correctly applies Grünbaum's theorem — Lemma 4.1's shrinkage argument only uses optimality with respect to ŵ_t, not w*, which the authors exploit in the corrupted case.

The corruption-robust extension (Section 5) is elegant: detecting corruption through cycle formation in the directed graph ([d], A_t) (Lemma 5.1) combined with the no-regret condition (Lemma 5.2) yields O((C+1)d log d) without prior knowledge of C. The restart-counting argument is correct since restart-triggering intervals are disjoint and each must contain a corrupted round.

The paper is well-written and well-organized: Table 1 positions the contribution precisely, the progression from warm-up (Section 3) to the refined algorithm (Section 4) aids comprehension, and Figure 2 gives a helpful illustration of how corruption detection works.

Practical computational aspects are addressed honestly: the #P-hardness of the exact centroid is acknowledged, with the standard randomized approximation cited, and per-round complexity of the warm-up algorithm (topological sort, O(d²)) is given.
weaknesses: The headline open question is only partially resolved: the finite polynomial regret bound holds under the M-convexity restriction, while the general polyhedral setting (where only exp(O(d log d)) or O(d log T) bounds are known) remains open. M-convexity is doing substantial work, and the paper does not give evidence (even informal) about whether the techniques could extend beyond this class, e.g., to general matroid intersection or other exchange structures.

The O(log d) gap between the O(d log d) upper bound and the Ω(d) lower bound is left open; for a result whose main selling point is dimension optimality up to logs, this is a modest but real incompleteness.

The contribution is a synthesis of largely standard tools — the pairwise-ordering/mistake-counting idea, the Grünbaum volume argument from contextual search (Gollapudi et al., 2021; Paes Leme & Schneider, 2022), and the restart paradigm from corruption-robust bandits — combined with the classical Murota characterization (Proposition 2.4). The novelty lies in the combination rather than in fundamentally new techniques.

The treatment of Assumption 2.2.2 (distinct components of w*) via 'arbitrarily small perturbation' is somewhat hand-wavy: the argument that the learner attaining the same regret under perturbed w* transfers to tied w* is asserted through Lipschitz continuity but not formalized, and similarly the tie-breaking/perturbation interaction with the approximate centroid computation (footnote 4) is handled by citation rather than proof.

The practical significance of removing the log T dependence is arguable: O(d log T) bounds from Sakaue et al. (2025b) are already mild, so the motivation rests mainly on resolving a theoretically posed open problem rather than on a new application capability. There are no experiments (acceptable for a theory paper, but a small-scale illustration of mistake counts on matroid instances would have strengthened the paper).

The corruption model counts rounds with any suboptimal action (C corruptions), which is more restrictive than the cumulative-suboptimality model of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the authors honestly flag this as future work, but it limits the reach of the robustness result.

strengths: Resolves a genuinely open question (partially): the paper establishes the first finite, polynomial-in-d regret bound of O(d log d) for online inverse linear optimization under M-convex action sets, improving on the prior dichotomy of O(d log T) (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Sakaue et al. 2025b) versus the practically useless exp(O(d log d)) bound, and matching the known Ω(d) lower bound up to a log d factor.

The technical core is clean and convincing: the local exchange characterization of optimal solutions on M-convex sets (Proposition 2.4) is combined with a Grünbaum-based volume argument (Lemma 4.1) and the Freudenthal triangulation into d! order simplices to bound the number of mistake rounds. I verified the key proofs (Theorems 3.1, 4.2, 5.3; Lemmas 4.1, 5.1, 5.2) and found them correct, including the subtlety that Lemma 4.1 does not require optimality of the observed action, which is essential for the corruption analysis.

The corruption-robust extension is elegant: monitoring acyclicity of the directed graph ([d], A_t) yields a restart-based algorithm achieving O((C+1)d log d) without prior knowledge of C, with each restart provably consuming at least one corrupted round (Lemma 5.1). This offers an alternative to the parallel-copies framework of Gupta et al. (2025).

The paper is well written and well organized: the warm-up O(d²) algorithm builds intuition before the refined analysis; assumptions (bounded per-round regret, distinct components of w*) are explicitly stated and justified; computational issues (e.g., #P-hardness of computing the exact center of gravity, resolved via randomized approximation) are discussed honestly; and Figure 2 usefully illustrates the corruption-detection mechanism.

The Ω(d) lower bound for the M-convex case, via embedding M♮-convex line-segment instances into M-convex sets in Z^{d+1}, shows the upper bound is tight up to a log factor and confirms the M-convexity restriction does not trivialize the problem.
weaknesses: No empirical evaluation. The paper motivates M-convexity by practical combinatorial applications (matroids, resource allocation), but provides no experiments demonstrating the algorithm's practical behavior, regret profiles, or runtime with approximate centroid computations, leaving practical impact unverified.

The novelty is primarily in the synthesis rather than the techniques: the volume/halving argument is standard in contextual search, and the restart mechanism for corruption robustness is a known pattern. The contribution rests on recognizing that M-convexity supplies the exchange structure needed to make these tools yield finite bounds; this is genuine but modest in methodological originality.

The corruption model is narrower than the most relevant prior work: it counts corrupted rounds rather than measuring cumulative suboptimality of corrupted actions as in Sakaue et al. (2025b). The authors acknowledge this gap, but it limits comparability of the O((C+1)d log d) guarantee.

Several quantities are hidden in constants and assumptions: per-round regret is assumed O(1) and the sizes of feasible/decision sets are treated as constants (deferring to Sakaue et al. 2025b, Appendix A), and the lower-bound instance requires dimension d+1 for an Ω(d) bound stated in terms of d. These are standard simplifications but reduce the precision of the practical implications.

The result is specialized to M-convex (integer-lattice) action sets; the general polyhedral case, which the paper itself argues is the genuinely challenging regime, remains open, so the open question is only partially resolved.

The exact computation of the center of gravity is #P-hard even for the order-simplex polytopes arising here, so the O(d log d) guarantee in practice relies on randomized approximate computation (with only a brief pointer to approximate Grünbaum results); a more careful treatment of how approximation errors propagate through the mistake count would strengthen the analysis.

strengths: The paper resolves (partially) a genuine open question in the literature on online inverse linear optimization / contextual recommendation: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in the dimension d is achievable. The O(d log d) bound under M-convex action sets (which subsume matroid bases, a broad and practically relevant class) is a clean and meaningful advance over the prior exp(O(d log d)) and O(d log T) bounds.

The main proof is elegant and appears technically correct: the warm-up O(d^2) analysis via pairwise orderings (Theorem 3.1) is carefully justified through Murota's optimality characterization (Proposition 2.4), and the refinement to O(d log d) via a Grünbaum-based volume argument (Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2) with the Freudenthal triangulation giving Vol >= 1/d! is well executed. I checked the key volume-shrinkage and order-simplex arguments and found no gaps.

The corruption-robust extension is a nice conceptual contribution: monitoring acyclicity of the directed graph induced by feedback (Lemma 5.1) yields an adaptive restart mechanism achieving O((C+1)d log d) without prior knowledge of C, complementing the parallel-copies approach of Gupta et al. (2025). The illustration in Figure 2 clarifies the mechanism.

The paper provides a matching lower bound: the Omega(d) lower bound is carefully adapted to the M-convex setting via the standard M♮-convex-to-M-convex embedding, showing the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor.

Reproducibility and honesty are good: Appendix A gives a polynomial-time approximate center-of-gravity implementation with a careful account of the randomization error (showing expected regret is preserved), Appendix B details oracle-based computational costs, Appendix D honestly discusses the distinct-components assumption and where it is essential, and a synthetic experiment compares against ONS and OGD baselines.
The paper is clearly written, with an honest limitations/future-work discussion (remaining log d gap, restricted corruption model, relation to preference feedback).
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely in synthesis rather than invention: the volume argument is imported from contextual search (Gollapudi et al., 2021; Paes Leme and Schneider, 2022), and the structural result (Proposition 2.4) is from Murota (2003). The contribution is the correct combination with the M-convex structure, which is valuable but incremental relative to the closest prior work (Sakaue et al., 2025b).

The practical relevance of the O(d log d) algorithm is limited by computational cost: exact center-of-gravity computation is #P-hard, and the approximate implementation costs O~(d^6 log d * log T) per round, which is quite heavy (acknowledged by the authors).

The corruption model counts the number of corrupted rounds rather than cumulative suboptimality, which is weaker than the model of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the corruption-robust bound also relies on the distinctness of components of w*, a somewhat non-standard assumption. Both limitations are acknowledged but constrain the reach of the robust result.

Empirical evidence is limited to a single small synthetic setting (d = 20, uniform matroids, T = 5000, five trials); it is illustrative rather than convincing, and the code URL appears to be missing/blank in the manuscript (Appendix C: 'available at .').
The assumptions that the per-round regret is O(1) and that the learner knows (or observes) X_t are standard simplifications, but they restrict generality of the reported bounds.

strengths: The paper partially resolves a genuine open question in the literature: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in d is achievable in online inverse linear optimization. The O(d log d) bound under M-convex action sets improves on the exponential exp(O(d log d)) bound of Gollapudi et al. (2021) and removes the log T dependence of prior logarithmic-in-T bounds, and Table 1 positions the contribution clearly against prior work.

The core analysis is clean and, as far as I could verify, technically sound. The warm-up O(d^2) argument (Theorem 3.1) via Proposition 2.4 is simple and correct, and the upgrade to O(d log d) via Grünbaum's theorem and the Freudenthal triangulation/order-simplex decomposition (Lemma 4.1, Theorem 4.2) is a well-executed volume argument. The claim that Lemma 4.1 does not rely on the optimality of observed actions is verified by the proof, and this is what makes the corruption extension work.

The corruption-robust extension is elegant: monitoring acyclicity of the directed graph induced by feedback (Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2) gives corruption detection without knowledge of C, and the O((C+1)d log d) bound is derived with a careful restart argument. Figure 2 gives a helpful illustration of delayed corruption detection.

The Ω(d) lower bound for the M-convex case (Theorem 6.1), obtained by embedding M♮-convex line-segment instances via the standard M♮-to-M transformation, shows the upper bound is tight up to a log d factor and confirms M-convexity does not trivialize the problem.

Computational aspects are treated seriously: Appendix A gives a polynomial-time randomized implementation with a careful check that approximate centers of gravity preserve the volume-decrease argument, and Appendix B details per-round costs under standard oracle models (including the matroid special case). Appendix D honestly explains why the distinctness assumption on components of w* is needed in the corrupted case and how ties can be removed in the uncorrupted case.
weaknesses: The central technical machinery (volume/Grünbaum arguments for pairwise order learning) is imported from the contextual search/recommendation literature (Gollapudi et al. 2021; Paes Leme and Schneider 2022). The novelty lies in synthesizing this with M-convexity rather than in fundamentally new techniques, which limits the methodological impact.

The practical relevance of the O(d log d) algorithm is questionable: exact center-of-gravity computation is #P-hard even for this polytope class, and the randomized implementation costs Õ(d^6 log d · log T) per round. The only empirical evidence is a small synthetic experiment (d = 20, uniform matroids, T = 5000, five trials) in Appendix C; no experiments with corruption, no comparison in the corrupted regime, and the code-availability link in Appendix C is left blank ("available at ."), which harms reproducibility.

The improvement is confined to M-convex feasible sets; the general open question (finite polynomial regret for arbitrary feasible sets) remains unresolved, and the paper is explicit that this is only a partial resolution. Additionally, the corruption-robust result requires the distinct-components assumption on w* (Assumption 2.2), which cannot be removed with the current detection mechanism (Appendix D), further narrowing the corrupted-case guarantee.

The corruption model counts the number of non-optimal rounds, which is less general than the cumulative-suboptimality corruption framework of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the paper acknowledges this but does not bridge the gap.

The regret metric, while standard in this line of work, is non-standard relative to usual online learning: the learner never actually commits an action and regret is measured against the agent's observed action. The paper defends this in Remark 2.1, but readers from the broader ICML community may find the setting's practical motivation thin, and the paper's own discussion in Section 7 concedes that settings where observed actions are generated by online learners would require additional ideas.

Several minor presentation issues: the assumption that the learner knows Xt at the start of the round is deferred with a brief remark; the constant-factor analysis with perturbations for tie-breaking (footnotes 4-5) is heuristic until checked against the approximate Grünbaum result in Appendix A.

strengths: The paper partially resolves a clearly stated open question in online inverse linear optimization: whether a finite regret bound polynomial in the dimension d is achievable. The O(d log d) bound under M-convex action sets is a meaningful, natural contribution, and the accompanying Ω(d) lower bound shows the result is tight up to a log d factor.

The technical development is clean and convincing: the warm-up O(d^2) analysis via Proposition 2.4 (Murota's optimality characterization) is transparent, and the refinement to O(d log d) via a Grünbaum-type volume argument over order simplices is elegant and well-executed. The proofs I checked (Theorems 3.1, 4.2, 5.3, Lemma 5.1, Theorem 6.1) appear correct.

The corruption-robust extension is a genuinely nice idea: monitoring acyclicity of the directed graph ([d], A_t) to detect corruptions adaptively, with restarts, yields O((C+1)d log d) regret without prior knowledge of C. Lemma 5.1 and Figure 2 make the mechanism easy to follow.

The paper is honest and thorough about assumptions and limitations: Assumption 2.2 is discussed, Appendix D carefully explains where distinctness of w*'s components is and is not needed, Appendix A gives a polynomial-time approximate implementation with a rigorous randomized regret analysis, and Appendix B details oracle-based computational costs.

The paper is well organized and clearly written, with an accurate related-work section that positions the contribution relative to contextual search/pricing (e.g., Gollapudi et al. 2021, Gupta et al. 2025) and explains what is genuinely new (synthesizing the volume argument with M-convex structure rather than the technique alone).
weaknesses: Empirical evaluation is very limited: a single synthetic experiment on time-varying uniform matroids with d=20, T=5000, and only two baselines. There are no experiments on general M-convex sets (e.g., partition matroids, integer lattice settings from Example 2), no corruption-robust experiment for Algorithm 2, and the code availability URL is left blank ('available at .'), which hurts reproducibility.

The practicality of the O(d log d) algorithm is questionable: exact center-of-gravity computation is #P-hard, and the approximate hit-and-run implementation costs Õ(d^6 log d · log(1/δ)) per round, which is steep. The small-scale experiment partially mitigates this, but scalability beyond small d remains unaddressed.

The corrupted-setting analysis requires distinct components of w* (ties would make directed cycles ambiguous, as discussed in Appendix D and footnote 7), so the corruption-robust guarantee holds under a somewhat restrictive assumption that is not fully removed. Additionally, the corruption model counts corrupted rounds rather than cumulative suboptimality, which is weaker than the framework of Sakaue et al. (2025b); the authors acknowledge this as future work.

The contribution is a specialization: the polynomial finite bound is established only under M-convexity, so the general open question (polynomial-in-d finite regret for arbitrary polyhedral action sets) remains open. The work is also partly a synthesis of known tools (volume arguments from contextual pricing, Murota's optimality characterization, restart-based corruption handling), so its originality lies in the combination and the new corruption-detection mechanism rather than entirely new techniques.

The Ω(d) lower bound (Theorem 6.1) is explicitly an adaptation of Sakaue et al. (2025b, Theorem 5.1) via a standard M♮-convex to M-convex embedding; while needed for completeness, it is not a substantially new technical contribution.
